clue.text: The love of money, according to St. Paul

definitions.text: The love of money, according to St. Paul

parts.words: The love of money, according to St. Paul
parts.note: St Paul's first letter to Timothy says the love of money is the source from which every kind of wickedness grows; the clue asks for that phrase

explanation.surface: A churchgoer quotes the apostle's warning about greed.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is 1 Timothy 6:10: 'the love of money is the root of all evil'. The clue gives the first half of the saying and asks for the second.
explanation.definitionFit: In the King James Bible, Paul calls greed for wealth the source of every wickedness, so the phrase completes his saying.

clue.text: Cleric somehow never limited by colour

indicators.note: something limited by a border is enclosed by it, so the colour word wraps round the other letters

parts.note: red is a colour

indicators.note: done somehow means done in some unspecified way, so the letters of 'never' are rearranged

explanation.surface: A churchman whose life is always bounded by his colour, perhaps the scarlet of a cardinal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'limited by' sounds like a restriction on behaviour; here it means enclosed, the colour wrapping round the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman is addressed by this title, so it serves as a noun for a member of the clergy.

clue.text: Capital means of getting about

parts.note: capital reads as the British capital city, and the means of getting about is its public network of buses and Underground trains

explanation.definitionFit: This was the name of the public body running buses and the Tube in Britain's capital city.

clue.text: Top class scholar?

parts.note: rather than the best student in a class, read top as the senior pupil chosen to lead a whole school

explanation.walkthrough: In British schools one senior pupil is appointed to lead and represent the others; 'top class' suggests academic excellence instead.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools the senior pupil appointed to lead the student body holds this title.

clue.text: County town getting equal in London

parts.note: Leicester is the county town of Leicestershire
square means level or equal, as in all square

explanation.surface: A Midlands town draws level with something in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: LEICESTER SQUARE is a famous square in London's West End, home to cinemas; a county town is the administrative centre of an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a well-known public place found in the British capital's West End.

clue.text: Good man, some say wonderful.

definitions.meaning: a clergyman or theologian, a godly person
colloquially, '...' means delightful or marvellous, which is why only some people say it

explanation.walkthrough: 'some say' marks the second sense as a colloquial usage, the gushing 'simply divine'.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word means a churchman; as gushing slang adjective it means heavenly or delightful.

clue.text: … but not in a lowdown place

indicators.note: the word that follows is to be left out of the word carried over from the clue before

parts.note: the ellipsis carries on from the previous clue, whose answer is the starting word

explanation.surface: A continuation that disowns the previous sentiment: not wonderful, just a seedy spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 6 down, DIVINE; 'but not in' removes IN from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dive is slang for a seedy bar or club, a disreputable venue.

clue.text: Drill to tax one's patience

definitions.meaning: to make a hole with a drill

explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both making a hole with a rotating tool and tiring someone through tedium.

clue.text: Three-quarters of 8 in aggregate

indicators.note: three of the word's four letters are kept, so one letter goes from the front

parts.note: the answer to 8 across

explanation.surface: A number puzzle about taking a fraction of a total.
explanation.walkthrough: 8 across is BORE; keeping three of its four letters drops the B.
explanation.definitionFit: Ore is rock containing metal, a mineral mass or aggregate mined for extraction.

clue.text: Panacea a high priest gives king on the side

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing on another follows it, so the king comes after the side

parts.note: Eli was the high priest who raised Samuel in the Bible
XI, eleven, is a team or side in cricket or football
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A cure-all that a priest hands to a monarch, slipped to him on the quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the side' suggests secrecy; here the side is a team of eleven, XI, with R after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An elixir is a supposed cure for every ill, the same idea as a universal remedy.

clue.text: Be there at the start and finish

indicators.note: the start of the word is its opening letter only

parts.note: the finish of something is its end

explanation.surface: An instruction to be present from the beginning to the close of an event.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend an event is to be present at it.

clue.text: Taken in by a form of vice, deed

indicators.note: the clue's closing 'indeed' reads as 'in deed', and one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a form of something is a reshaped version, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone duped by a kind of wickedness, truly.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's last word is read as two, 'in deed', so the rearranged vice sits inside the deed.
explanation.definitionFit: To be taken in is to be fooled, tricked or misled.

clue.text: P M is back, eats somehow, takes a nap

parts.note: p.m. is the time after noon

indicators.note: back means the little word is read the other way round
done somehow means done in some unspecified way, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister returns, has a meal and then dozes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'P M' looks like the Prime Minister; it is post meridiem. 'back' turns IS to SI, and 'somehow' rearranges EATS to ESTA.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is a short sleep taken in the early part of the day after lunch.

clue.text: Can be used to describe money

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a sealed metal food container and, in dated slang, cash.

clue.text: First woman to give trouble with the box?

definitions.text: First woman to give trouble with the box?

parts.words: First woman to give trouble with the box?
parts.note: in Greek myth the first woman opened a jar or box and let all the world's troubles out; the box could also be read as television

explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth she was the first woman created, and opening her jar released every evil.

clue.text: See 1
Plant seaman never can find

indicators.note: the letters can be rearranged to find a new word, so they are shuffled

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A garden plant that a sailor can never seem to locate.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbena is a flowering garden plant, also called vervain.

clue.text: One can take it to be agriculturally productive

parts.note: taken as written
arable land is suitable for growing crops

explanation.surface: A farmer's optimism that some land will yield good crops.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as a description: something one can take, or put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tolerable is something a person is able to endure.

clue.text: Feeling aroused by an Oriental action

parts.note: E, for east, means Oriental
motion is movement or action

explanation.surface: A passion stirred up by something done by someone from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is a strong sentiment, such as love or anger.

clue.text: Slips that cause some dirty looks?

definitions.text: Slips that cause some dirty looks?

parts.words: Slips that cause some dirty looks?
parts.note: slips are errors, and dirty looks are glares; obvious errors are described with a word meaning both conspicuous and staring angrily

explanation.definitionFit: Obvious blunders are called glaring, and 'glaring' also means scowling at someone.

clue.text: Least common form of arrest

indicators.note: a form of a word is a reshaped version, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rare kind of police detention.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rarest is the most infrequent or least often seen.

clue.text: Metropolitan area one may find genial

indicators.note: one may find the word within these letters by rearranging them

explanation.surface: A friendly suburb of the city.
explanation.walkthrough: EALING is a district of west London, famous for its film studios.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a borough of Greater London, an area of the metropolis.

clue.text: About right in the main, it finally becomes battered

indicators.note: finally places this little word at the very end of the answer
one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: the deep and the main are both poetic words for the sea
C, for circa, means about
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ship at sea, about to be right, ends up battered by the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the main' is a poetic name for the sea, the deep; 'finally' puts the last piece at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Something decrepit is worn out and dilapidated through age or ill use.

clue.text: See 1
Classy fur that can be worn

parts.note: U means upper-class, in the dated British sense of correct social usage
sable is a costly fur

explanation.surface: An upmarket fur coat fit to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: U as upper-class comes from 1950s British debate on 'U and non-U' speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Something usable is fit for service, and clothing is put to use by wearing it.

clue.text: Skiers put off course by common word of mouth

indicators.note: put off course means sent awry, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Skiers sent astray by gossip passed around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'word of mouth' looks like gossip, but 'common word' means a slang word, here for the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Kisser is slang for the mouth or face, so it is a vulgar word for that body part.

clue.text: One in a racing eight, albeit sounds like 9

indicators.note: the answer is said the same way as the other word

parts.note: the answer to 9 across

explanation.surface: A rower's blade in a racing boat, homophone of a metal-bearing rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 across is ORE, which is pronounced like OAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing eight is a rowing boat propelled by eight long blades.

clue.text: Cat, and where it's likely to get a birdie one hears

indicators.note: the answer is pronounced like the word described

parts.words: where it's likely to get a birdie
parts.note: a birdie is one under par in golf, which happens on a golf course, the links

explanation.surface: A wild cat lurking where birds are easy prey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'birdie' suggests a small bird for the cat to catch; it is the golf score, and links is a seaside golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: The lynx is a short-tailed wild feline.
